subsection: 7. Economic consequences of decolonisation: the Lomé Conventions, trade, aid and famine, and Nyerere's ujamaa

notes.b: Most African states became independent between the late 1950s and 1960s, but political independence did not bring economic independence. Colonial rule had built economies to export raw materials to Europe, and those structures outlived the flags coming down.
points: Colonial economies were organised around cash crops (crops grown for sale abroad, not for local food) and minerals: cocoa in the Gold Coast, groundnuts in Senegal, cotton in Uganda and copper in Katanga.

Railways and ports were built to carry exports to the coast, so most African transport networks linked interior mines and farms to ports rather than to each other. This made trade between neighbouring African countries hard after independence.
Colonial powers controlled trade through their own companies and currencies, so African states inherited trading patterns that tied them to a few European markets.

Colonial governments in the Belgian Congo and Portuguese Mozambique forced peasants to grow set quantities of cotton, which was bought at fixed low prices. Farmers therefore had little incentive or income to improve their position.
Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued from 1950 that the terms of trade (the ratio of export prices to import prices) tend to move against primary producers, those who sell raw materials.
African countries therefore have to export more to buy the same manufactured goods, and commodity prices fell sharply in the 1980s.

Dependence on one or two commodities made African economies vulnerable to price falls, because a single bad year in world markets cut national income. Examples are copper prices in the mid-1970s and cocoa and coffee prices in the 1980s.

Multinational companies (firms operating in many countries) such as Unilever's United Africa Company, Shell-BP in Nigerian oil and Union Minière du Haut-Katanga in Katanga copper kept control of trade, oil and mining after independence.
This is why the topic is linked to the idea of a transnational economy, in which trade, finance and production cross borders through multinationals and lenders.
notes.tip: For essays on the economic effects of decolonisation, start from the colonial structures: export crops, export-geared transport and a few commodities. Then link each later problem back to them.

notes.b: The European Economic Community (EEC), created by the Treaty of Rome in 1957, set up trade and aid agreements with former African colonies. These grew from an association of colonies into the Lomé Conventions, which offered a new kind of deal.
points: The Treaty of Rome of 1957 associated the overseas territories of the EEC members, mostly in Africa, with the Community. This gave those territories special trading links with the new EEC.

The Yaoundé Convention of 1963 (with a second in 1969) between the EEC and 18 associated African states gave their exports duty-free access to European markets in return for limited reciprocal opening of their own markets.

Lomé I was signed on 28 February 1975 in Lomé, Togo, between the EEC (then nine members) and 46 African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states. The ACP group was formally founded by the Georgetown Agreement in June 1975.
Britain's entry in 1973 had brought in Commonwealth countries, so the group was wider than the Yaoundé states.

Lomé I gave ACP exports largely duty-free access to the EEC without requiring reciprocal concessions, meaning the ACP did not have to open its own markets in return. This was a new departure in trade relations, though agricultural products covered by the Common Agricultural Policy were treated less generously.

STABEX was a fund set up under Lomé I to compensate ACP countries when earnings from listed agricultural exports fell below a reference level. It cushioned the price falls that made single-commodity economies so vulnerable.
Lomé I also included a Sugar Protocol, which guaranteed quotas for ACP sugar at European prices. Lomé II (1979) added SYSMIN, support for mineral exporters.

Later Conventions were signed in 1979 (Lomé II), 1984 (Lomé III) and 1989 (Lomé IV). Lomé IV was revised in the mid-1990s, when human rights became an essential element, and the Conventions were replaced by the Cotonou Agreement, signed in 2000.
The Conventions had limits. ACP exports stayed concentrated on a few commodities despite the preferences, and the aid element was small against the needs of the countries involved.
notes.tip: Lomé questions ask who signed (the EEC and the ACP states), when (1975), what was new (non-reciprocal access), STABEX, and a limit (continued commodity dependence). Do not confuse Yaoundé (1963, 1969, 18 African states, reciprocal terms) with Lomé (ACP states, non-reciprocal).

notes.h: Debt, the IMF and the World Bank, 1970s-1980s
notes.b: In the 1970s many African governments borrowed heavily, and in the 1980s they could not repay. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank then used their loans to push through economic reforms that proved very controversial.
points: The IMF and the World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference in the United States in July 1944. The IMF lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems (when they spend more abroad than they earn), with conditions attached, while the World Bank funds development projects.

Oil price rises in 1973 and 1979 raised import costs for oil-importing African states, so many governments borrowed heavily from banks and international lenders in the 1970s to keep paying their bills.

When interest rates rose in the early 1980s and commodity prices fell, African countries earned less and owed more, so they struggled to repay. Mexico's default in August 1982 marked the start of the wider debt crisis.

From the early 1980s the IMF and World Bank made new loans conditional on structural adjustment programmes: devaluation (making the currency cheaper), cuts in public spending, removal of subsidies and the sale of state enterprises (privatisation).

The World Bank's report Accelerated Development in Sub-Saharan Africa, known as the Berg Report (1981), blamed African governments' own policies: overvalued currencies, state marketing boards and neglect of agriculture.
Critics argued that structural adjustment cut spending on health and education, so the poor paid for it. UNICEF's 1987 report Adjustment with a Human Face made the case for protecting the poor.

Ghana under Jerry Rawlings adopted an IMF-backed Economic Recovery Programme from 1983. Supporters presented it as an early success, but this view was contested because the programme brought hardship.
notes.tip: Keep the IMF (balance-of-payments loans) and the World Bank (development projects) apart, and give both the Berg Report view and the critics' view of structural adjustment.

notes.b: Aid was meant to help new states develop, but it came with strings and often kept them tied to the same partners as before. Examiners reward answers that weigh both its benefits and its costs.
points: Aid came in two forms: bilateral aid, given government to government by a donor state, and multilateral aid, channelled through bodies such as the World Bank and the UN.
Tied aid required recipients to spend the money on goods and services from the donor country, which increased its cost and reduced its value to the recipient.
Many former colonies received aid from their former rulers, so aid often reinforced existing trade and political links rather than diversifying them.
Aid was criticised for supporting corrupt or authoritarian governments, such as Mobutu's Zaire, which received large Western aid, and for creating dependence on donors for budgets and food.

Some African governments tried to reduce dependence by promoting local industry and regional trade, but many national markets remained small and fragmented, so it was hard for new factories to find enough customers.
The United Nations General Assembly set a target in 1970 that rich countries give 0.7 per cent of national income as aid. Most donors did not reach it.

Cold War rivalry shaped aid because both superpowers courted African states. China built the TAZARA railway from Zambia to the Tanzanian port of Dar es Salaam, with Chinese finance and labour, between about 1970 and 1975. The Soviet Union and the United States each aided their allies.
notes.tip: When evaluating aid, give both sides: relief, schools and health on one hand; tied aid, dependence and support for corrupt regimes on the other. Do not confuse aid with trade preferences such as Lomé.

notes.h: Famine: Biafra, the Sahel and Ethiopia
notes.b: Famines in the post-colonial period were caused by war, drought and state policy, and they drew international relief efforts. Public reaction in Europe and North America, helped by television and photographs, shaped the later charity movement.
points: During the Biafran War (1967-70), blockade and fighting caused a famine in Biafra in 1968-70, and images of starving children drew wide attention in Europe and North America.

Relief flights into Biafra mostly ran at night from São Tomé to the Uli airstrip, and they were limited by the federal government's control of the airspace. In June 1969 a Red Cross aircraft was shot down.

A drought in the Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s caused famine across Mali, Niger, Chad, Mauritania, Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) and Senegal, with large loss of livestock.
The Wollo famine of 1972-74 was in Ethiopia, not the Sahel proper. It helped bring down Emperor Haile Selassie, who was deposed in 1974, because it showed his government's failure to respond.

The Ethiopian famine of 1983-85 killed hundreds of thousands, with estimates from about 300,000 to one million. Drought combined with the policies of the Derg (the military regime) and the wars in Eritrea and Tigray. A BBC report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 brought it to Western attention.

The British singer Bob Geldof organised the Band Aid charity single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?', released in December 1984. The Live Aid concerts in London and Philadelphia on 13 July 1985 followed, and together they raised about 150 million pounds over time for famine relief.
Famine relief was also criticised for distorting local markets, because free food undercut local farmers, and for prolonging wars when food aid went to armed groups.
The Ethiopian government's resettlement programme of 1984-86 moved about 600,000 people from the drought-hit north. Many thousands died, though estimates vary.
notes.tip: Link causes (war, drought, state policy) to outcomes (relief, Band Aid, Live Aid), and add criticisms of relief for a better answer. Keep Band Aid (the 1984 single) apart from Live Aid (the 1985 concerts), and Biafra (1968-70) apart from the Sahel (1970s) and Ethiopia (1983-85).

notes.b: Much famine relief and development work was done not by governments but by voluntary organisations, and several of the best known were Irish. Their growth followed the famines, especially Biafra.
points: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are non-state charities and campaigning bodies that deliver aid and work on development projects.
Oxfam was founded in Oxford in 1942 as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief, and it later expanded into development work across Africa and Asia.
Concern was founded in Dublin in 1968 by John and Kay O'Loughlin Kennedy in response to the Biafran famine, and it became one of Ireland's main aid agencies.

Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Catholic bishops of Ireland as the Irish Catholic development agency, and it works through local partners in Africa. Its annual Lenten campaign raised money and awareness in Irish parishes and became one of the best-known development campaigns in Ireland.
GOAL was founded in Dublin in 1977 by John O'Shea. Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in France in 1971 by doctors, some of whom had worked in Biafra.

NGOs distinguish between emergency relief (short-term help in a crisis) and long-term development (building lasting ability to feed and educate people). Many shifted in the 1980s towards community projects and advocacy, meaning campaigning for change.
The Irish government began an official aid programme in 1974, and Irish missionary orders had long worked in Africa.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level questions ask you to define NGO and to name an Irish agency with its founding date: Concern 1968, Trócaire 1973, GOAL 1977. Do not mix up Concern (Irish, 1968), Oxfam (British, 1942) and Trócaire (Irish Catholic, 1973).

notes.h: Nyerere's ujamaa: the Arusha Declaration to villagisation
notes.b: Julius Nyerere, leader of Tanzania, tried to build African socialism through state control and rural villages. The policy began as a voluntary programme and turned compulsory.
points: The Arusha Declaration of 5 February 1967, issued by TANU (the ruling party) under Julius Nyerere, committed Tanzania to ujamaa (familyhood, or African socialism), self-reliance and state control of the main means of production.
The government nationalised the banks and major industries in 1967. It also introduced 'Education for Self-Reliance' in 1967, a policy to shape schooling around rural work and life.

TANU's Mwongozo (guidelines) of 1971 required party members to work for their living and to avoid exploitation and privilege. This was a leadership code meant to stop party leaders becoming a new elite.
The ujamaa villages were voluntary cooperative settlements at first. But from 1973-74 the government moved millions of people into villages, often by force, in a policy called villagisation.

Villagisation disrupted farming because families were moved away from their fields, and food shortages followed. Do not confuse ujamaa (the policy), villagisation (the compulsory phase) and the Arusha Declaration (the 1967 statement).
notes.tip: Strong answers date the Arusha Declaration (1967), villagisation (1973-74) and the reversal (1986), and keep the three terms apart. For Ordinary Level, be ready to state what the Arusha Declaration committed Tanzania to.

notes.b: Ujamaa produced real gains in education and health but also economic decline. How Nyerere is judged depends on which of these is stressed.
points: Universal primary education, launched in 1974, aimed to put every child in school by 1977, and primary enrolment rose rapidly. Tanzania's literacy and primary schooling expanded markedly, which showed what a poor country could achieve in social services.

Villagisation was not the only cause of the crisis. The oil price rise of 1979, drought and the cost of the war to overthrow Idi Amin of Uganda in 1978-79 added to it. Tanzania had to import food, and the economy was in decline by the early 1980s.

Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985. His successor Ali Hassan Mwinyi accepted an IMF agreement in 1986 that reversed many of the socialist policies, which shows how far ujamaa had failed economically.
Nyerere, known as Mwalimu (teacher), died in 1999. Supporters stress his gains in education, health and national unity and his refusal to rule by ethnic favour.
Critics stress the collapse of farm output, the use of compulsion and the one-party state, since Tanzania was ruled by TANU/CCM with no legal rival.
notes.tip: Essays on Nyerere reward a balanced verdict: gains in education, health and national unity against forced villagisation and economic decline.

notes.h: Key personality: a development worker in Africa (Aengus Finucane)
notes.b: Development workers, including missionaries, volunteers and agency staff, carried out most of the day-to-day aid work in rural Africa from the 1960s. Aengus Finucane is a documented Irish example.
points: Development workers came from churches, voluntary bodies such as Britain's Voluntary Service Overseas (1958), government programmes such as the American Peace Corps (1961), and NGOs such as Concern and Trócaire.
Aengus Finucane, an Irish Holy Ghost priest (Spiritan), worked in Biafra relief during the war, 1968-70, with Concern. He later led Concern as chief executive until 1997 and died in 2009.

Their typical work included well-digging, agricultural advice, primary health care and vaccination, the supply of food in famines, and training of local staff, so that communities could manage after the workers left.
Many arrived as young volunteers on short contracts, and they often lived in remote rural communities with limited access to medicine, transport and communications.

Their problems included poor roads and supplies, cultural misunderstandings with local communities, the risk of violence during civil wars, and the difficulty of keeping projects running after the donor left.
They were participants in the aid system but also witnesses to its results, and their reports were important sources for NGO campaigns in Europe and North America.

Contemporaries in Europe often saw development workers as humanitarian heroes, while some critics saw them as agents of dependence on foreign money. Historians have criticised 'top-down' development projects of the 1960s and 1970s, and they have praised the shift in the 1980s towards projects planned with local people.
Irish missionary orders such as the Holy Ghost Fathers and the Medical Missionaries of Mary ran schools, hospitals and clinics in Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania and elsewhere.
notes.tip: Questions on development workers ask about the problems they faced and the work they did. Use concrete problems (roads, supplies, cultural misunderstanding, war, projects collapsing after the donor left) and a named example.

notes.h: Assessment: did the economic legacy of decolonisation help Africa?
notes.b: The verdict is mixed, and examiners reward a stated judgement supported by paired achievements and limits. Colonial structures, debt, dependence and famine weigh against gains in health, education and trade terms.
points: Achievement: the Lomé Conventions gave ACP states preferential access to European markets and a stabilisation fund (STABEX), which was a recognised innovation in trade policy.
Limit: despite these trade preferences, most ACP exports stayed concentrated on a few primary commodities, and commodity prices fell in the 1980s.

Achievement: international health campaigns eradicated smallpox, whose last natural case was in Somalia in 1977 and which the World Health Organization declared eradicated in 1980. Aid and NGO work also improved access to water and primary schooling in many areas.
Limit: debt and structural adjustment left many governments cutting public services, and the famines of the 1970s and 1980s showed how fragile food supply remained.
Achievement: Tanzania's expansion of literacy and primary education showed what a government with limited resources could achieve in social services.
Limit: villagisation and the collapse of agricultural output showed that state-directed development could cause serious hardship.

Later view: Walter Rodney, in How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972), blamed colonial exploitation, while the World Bank's Berg Report of 1981 blamed domestic policies. Most historians now combine colonial legacies, falling commodity prices, Cold War pressures and government choices.
notes.tip: State your judgement early (largely damaging or mixed), then support it with paired points: colonial structures, debt, dependence and famine against some health, education and trade gains.

Tanzania's policy from 1973-74 of moving rural people into planned villages, often by compulsion, to carry out ujamaa.
Aid that the recipient must spend on goods and services from the donor country.
